Capital is flowing out of technology names and into the hard assets, baseload power generation, and silicon foundries required to sustain the artificial intelligence supercycle. The true bottleneck lies in the physical infrastructure required to keep hyperscale data centers from melting down. Constructing a portfolio from square one means acknowledging that digital expansion is strictly bound by power grids and silicon foundries. Capitalizing on today's technological growth requires a focus on the foundational hardware and power systems that enable next-generation processing. The AI ecosystem refuses to be held hostage by a single vendor. Buying the top of a monopoly often means the easy upside is gone, but the ongoing buildout of compute power offers multiple entry points. title: Five Dividend Giants Booted From The DJIA That Rewarded Patient Investors: (NYSE: MO), (NYSE: T), (NYSE: XOM), (NYSE: IP), (NYSE: PFE) - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By Ewan Scott | Jul 23, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis The Dow Jones Industrial Average is managed by S&P Dow Jones Indices, with composition changes determined by an index committee rather than any fixed formula or automatic screening process. Unlike the S&P 500, which uses largely rules-based, quantitative criteria, the Dow’s committee makes essentially editorial judgment calls on which companies belong in the 30-stock index. The S&P Dow Jones Indices Averages Committee is made up of full-time analysts and economists who weigh factors including reputation, sector balance, stock price distortions, and overall fit within the U.S. economy. Because the Dow is price-weighted rather than market-cap weighted, a stock with an unusually high or low price can distort the index’s calculations and trigger a membership change. A review of stocks removed from the Dow over the past several decades reveals that some ejected companies went on to soar in value while continuing to pay substantial dividends to shareholders. Altria (NYSE: MO), one of the world’s largest tobacco producers, was removed from the index in 2008, and shareholders who held through the transition saw their shares surge by more than 150% in the following years, excluding dividends, according to Kiplinger. Altria currently offers a 5.66% dividend yield and raised its quarterly dividend in the fall of 2025 by 3.9%, from $1.02 to $1.06 per share, marking its 57th consecutive annual dividend increase. AT&T (NYSE: T), the world’s fourth-largest telecommunications company by revenue, was removed from the Dow in 2015 to make room for Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), and currently carries a dividend yield of 5.06% with 13 analysts assigning the stock a Buy rating. Exxon Mobil (NYSE: XOM) was removed in August 2020 after a remarkable 92-year run on the index, displaced to make room for Salesforce (NYSE: CRM), yet continued raising its dividend and delivering strong total returns for investors. Exxon completed its acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources in 2024 in an all-stock transaction valued at $59.5 billion, creating the largest U.S. oilfield producer and securing a decade of low-cost production ahead. International Paper (NYSE: IP), which provides sustainable fiber-based packaging solutions across North America, Latin America, Europe, and North Africa, was removed from the Dow in April 2004 and subsequently rebounded approximately 25%, delivering total returns exceeding 100% when dividends are included, according to Kiplinger. The company currently offers a 5.09% dividend yield, and its product lines span corrugated packaging, solid fiber, retail displays, bulk packaging, and a full range of recycling solutions for retailers and e-commerce companies. Pfizer (NYSE: PFE), founded in 1849 in New York, was removed from the Dow in August 2020 alongside Exxon to accommodate Amgen (NASDAQ: AMGN), and currently pays a 6.93% dividend that has increased annually for the past 15 years. Pfizer anticipates full-year 2026 revenues in the range of $59.5 billion to $62.5 billion, though the outlook reflects an expected $1.5 billion decline in COVID-19 product sales and an additional $1.5 billion headwind from upcoming drug patent expirations. The broader pattern across these five stocks suggests that Dow removal does not necessarily signal a company’s decline, and income-focused investors willing to hold through transitions have historically been well rewarded. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: Chevron’s Best Stock Rally Since 2022 Faces China-Sized Problem - ExxonMobil Holdings (NYSE:XOM), Chevron - Benzinga
content: Chevron Corp. (NYSE:CVX) is on track for its strongest monthly performance since October 2022 as crude prices surged amid escalating tensions in the Middle East. The integrated oil major has climbed more than 18% in July. Peer Exxon Mobil Corp. (NYSE:XOM) rose 15% over the same window. Yet beneath the surface of the Middle East-driven rally, another force is quietly pointing in the opposite direction. The world’s largest crude importer has suddenly slashed oil purchases to levels not seen in nearly a decade, raising a difficult question for investors: once the geopolitical premium fades, will demand be strong enough to keep crude elevated? According to Jeffrey J. Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, China is no longer providing the demand support that oil producers were counting on. “The sharp decline in China’s crude oil imports is potentially more bearish than bullish for the global oil market, at least in the near term,” Roach said in a recent note. China’s June crude imports fell to just 29.27 million metric tons, or 7.12 million barrels per day, according to Chinese customs data cited by Reuters. That marked a 41.3% decline from a year earlier, another 12% drop from May, and the weakest daily import level since October 2016. For a country that has been responsible for a large share of incremental global oil demand over the past two decades, the decline is difficult to ignore. Roach believes investors may be underestimating what those numbers imply. “China is the world’s largest crude importer, so the big drop in recent months signals that one of the most important sources of global oil demand is not providing the support many producers were hoping for,” he added. China’s refinery utilization rate dropped to 57.72% in June, down 13.09 percentage points from a year earlier, suggesting refiners deliberately reduced crude purchases instead of merely struggling with shipping disruptions. Imports from the Middle East also fell to a 10-year low, while Iranian crude purchases declined about 40% from May to below 800,000 barrels per day. The current rally in crude has been built almost entirely on geopolitical risk. Markets have focused on potential supply disruptions across the Persian Gulf, assigning a premium to Brent and WTI prices. But demand ultimately determines whether higher prices can be sustained. Roach warned that weakening Chinese demand is colliding with rising global supply. “Weaker Chinese imports arrive at an awkward time for producers. OPEC+ has been gradually restoring production, and non-OPEC supply growth remains relatively healthy,” he said. If those trends continue, he believes the balance could quickly swing back toward excess supply. That outlook aligns with the latest forecast from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The agency expects oil markets to remain relatively tight through much of the third quarter because of recent geopolitical disruptions. After that adjustment period, however, it forecasts global markets returning to the oversupply conditions that existed before the conflict as production growth outpaces demand. For Chevron and Exxon investors, the key question is not whether crude prices can remain elevated for another few weeks. It is whether today’s geopolitical premium can survive a world in which the largest oil consumer is buying dramatically less crude while OPEC+ continues reopening the taps. The oil rally has been driven by supply fears. Its next move could be determined by demand. While retail investors react to the market, lawmakers are already positioning into specific stocks. title: .XOM Introduces Cinematic Debut Era with "Red Eyes Black Dragon" - buzzmusic
content:
Southern California alternative rock outfit .XOM is opening the door to its debut concept album, One Winged Angels, with the release of its emotionally charged lead single, "Red Eyes Black Dragon." Released independently through Moxley Records, the track serves as the first chapter of an ambitious narrative that unfolds across the entire album, blending alternative rock, post-hardcore, and cinematic storytelling into a cohesive world. Rather than approaching heartbreak as a standalone theme, "Red Eyes Black Dragon" explores the identity crisis that follows the end of a relationship. The song captures the unsettling realization that it's not just another person you've lost, but the version of yourself that existed alongside them. It's a nuanced perspective that immediately establishes the emotional depth at the heart of One Winged Angels. Musically, .XOM balances soaring melodic hooks with crushing guitars and explosive dynamics. Atmospheric passages give listeners room to absorb the lyrics before the heavier moments crash in, mirroring the emotional highs and lows that accompany grief, denial, and anger. The band's post-hardcore influences never overpower the songwriting, instead amplifying the weight of every line. One of the song's strongest elements is its recurring phrase, "Fall to pieces, go the distance." Introduced here as a rallying cry, the lyric evolves throughout the album, reflecting the changing mindset of its central character as the story progresses. It's a subtle but effective piece of world-building that rewards listeners willing to experience the project from beginning to end. As the first glimpse into One Winged Angels, "Red Eyes Black Dragon" succeeds in establishing both the band's sonic identity and creative ambition. With emotionally honest songwriting, immersive storytelling, and a clear commitment to building something larger than a collection of singles.XOM delivers a compelling introduction to what feels like the beginning of an exciting new chapter in modern alternative rock. "Red Eyes Black Dragon" introduces the emotional journey of One Winged Angels. Why did you choose this song to be listeners' first entry point into the album's story? Honestly, it was the first song we wrote for the album, so everything naturally went from there. We had all gone through breakups around the same time, and songwriting became a way to process those emotions. While we were talking about some of our favorite records growing up (The Black Parade, American Idiot, Songs for the Deaf,) our guitarist Gabriel jokingly challenged us to write our own “rock opera.” 

Somehow the joke turned into a real project. Ivan brought in the original concept for “Red Eyes,” and Dakota expanded on it with additional lyrics. While the entire story hadn’t been imagined yet, “Red Eyes Black Dragon” sets up a powerful opening. Musically, "Red Eyes Black Dragon" is rooted in our influences: 2000s emo, SoCal indie rock, and experimental post-hardcore. At times, even nods back to some of our earlier releases. Looking back now, it's the perfect opening chapter because it's the moment everything begins to be set in motion, both for the character and, in a lot of ways, for us as a band at the time. The album explores grief, identity, and healing through recurring characters and themes. How did you approach balancing cinematic world-building with lyrics that still feel deeply personal and relatable? We always wanted the emotions to feel real, even if the story itself became more dramatic. Most of the characters and situations are inspired by our own experiences, just pushed further into fictional territory. None of our own personal breakups were as dramatic as the album portrays, but the guilt, uncertainty, loneliness, and hope behind them absolutely were. Ironically, while we were recording, life started mirroring the album. 

Many of us dealt with accidents, more breakups, lineup changes, and a lot of unexpected setbacks. Suddenly the story we were writing didn't feel so fictional anymore. I feel that's what makes the record relatable. Even though it's told through recurring characters and imagery, it's really about something almost everyone experiences at some point. You can watch the version of your future you built fall apart and are left to figure out what’s left standing afterward. Your sound blends melodic alternative rock with post-hardcore intensity. How do you decide when a moment calls for restraint versus an explosive release of emotion? We've all been playing together in different projects for the better part of a decade. Naturally, we've developed a lot of trust and chemistry. We know each other's instincts and can usually tell where a song wants to go without saying much. We also believe the loud moments only work if you've earned them. If every song stays at one intensity, nothing really hits. The quieter sections give people a chance to sit with the lyrics and emotions, while the heavier moments become a cathartic release instead of just noise. A lot of that comes from jamming around shared influences and asking ourselves what best serves the song instead of trying to force a specific genre or sound. In live situations, it’s physical. The audience needs a vibe moment after moshing. The phrase "Fall to pieces, go the distance" changes meaning as the album unfolds. Was that evolution planned from the beginning, or did it develop naturally as you wrote the record? A little bit of both. We only had three or four songs written when we started, and the rest of the story developed naturally as we kept writing and recording. As the narrative expanded, we realized that phrase could evolve alongside the main character. At first it almost feels like a warning, but by the end of the album it becomes something much more hopeful. 

Sometimes falling apart is what forces you to become the person you're meant to be. "Fall to pieces, go the distance" became a reminder that you're ultimately the author of your own story. The words never change, but their meaning does, depending on where you are in your journey. As an independent band releasing a full concept album in an era dominated by singles, what gave you the confidence to invest in such an ambitious project, and what do you hope listeners discover by experiencing One Winged Angels from start to finish? Honestly, we wanted to challenge ourselves. We wanted to do something unique and true to ourselves and have it naturally stand out that way. It's easy to chase singles and algorithms, but we've always loved albums that reward you for listening all the way through. We wanted to make something people could get lost in, and it was so much fun building a backstory and lore and having it all connect from beginning to end. Being independent also gave us the freedom to build this world around the music instead of just releasing songs. We made physical CDs, artwork, merch, zines, collaborated with friends, and even incorporated local artists and mutual aid organizations into our release show. It became much bigger than we originally imagined. At its core, One Winged Angels is about surviving change. It's about losing the future you thought you were going to have, finding yourself at rock bottom, and discovering that healing is about becoming someone new if you let yourself. In a weird way, that's exactly what happened to us while making the album. We fell to pieces, went the distance, and somehow ended up in a better place than where we started.

title: Is Exxon Mobil's Recent Surge Sustainable Amid Middle East Tensions - Kavout | AI
content: Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock has been a standout performer in recent weeks, with shares trading at $154.19 as of March 2, 2026, up 1.11% on the day and nearing its 52-week high of $159.35. This impressive run, which saw the stock climb from $115.15 on November 30, 2025, to $152.50 by March 1, 2026—a 32.4% increase—is largely attributed to a dramatic shift in the global energy landscape. The "Midnight Hammer" crisis in the Middle East, characterized by retaliatory strikes and a de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has injected a significant risk premium into crude oil markets. This geopolitical shock has sent oil prices soaring, with WTI crude currently at $71.15 per barrel, having recently spiked towards $73 and Brent crude briefly touching $100 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for 20% of global seaborne oil, has seen shipping halted and war risk coverage cancelled by marine insurers, effectively stranding an estimated 15 million barrels per day (bpd) of global supply. This immediate supply disruption, combined with a perceived failure of OPEC+ to adequately increase production, has fueled a rapid "risk-off" rotation into hard assets like oil. The market's reaction on March 2, 2026, saw XOM and Occidental Petroleum (OXY) both climb 2.1% by midday, even as the broader S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite tumbled. This divergence underscores a fundamental reassessment of value in an uncertain geopolitical climate, where the "old economy" energy trade has become a defensive hedge. While the immediate catalyst is conflict, the underlying "AI Power Crunch"—the insatiable demand for energy to fuel massive data centers—is also contributing to a structural revaluation of energy companies. However, the sustainability of this surge hinges precariously on the resolution of the Strait of Hormuz standoff. Analysts warn that a diplomatic "off-ramp" within the next 72 hours could lead to a significant cooling of oil prices. Conversely, if the blockade persists, a "super-spike" toward $120 per barrel is possible, which would almost certainly tip the broader global economy into a recession by Q3 2026. This delicate balance means XOM's recent gains, while substantial, are tied to highly unpredictable global events. The current surge in oil prices provides a significant tailwind for Exxon Mobil's Q1 2026 earnings, potentially rewriting near-term cash flow math. Higher crude prices directly enhance the profitability of Exxon's Upstream segment, which saw a 41% increase in revenue in Q1 2025, including a remarkable 234% jump in its U.S. Upstream operations. This segment is particularly sensitive to commodity price fluctuations, making the current environment highly favorable for top-line growth and margin expansion. Despite a 6% decline in net profit and a 15% fall in EPS in Q1 2025 due to weaker refining margins and petrochemicals, the company demonstrated resilience later in the year. Exxon Mobil reported strong Q3 2025 earnings of $7.5 billion and $14.8 billion in cash flow, followed by a Q4 2025 EPS of $1.71, beating estimates. This consistent outperformance, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of earnings beats, suggests an underlying operational strength that can capitalize on improved market conditions. Analysts are already adjusting their expectations, with Bank of America raising ExxonMobil's price target from $135 to $151, reflecting confidence in enhanced future profitability due to the oil risk premium. The consensus Q1 2026 EPS is projected at approximately $1.53, a figure that could prove conservative if oil prices remain elevated throughout the quarter. Exxon's ability to generate substantial free cash flow, projected at $52 billion for the 2025-2026 period, further strengthens its financial position to navigate market dynamics. However, it's not a clear-cut picture. While Upstream benefits, the Energy Products (refining) and Chemical Products segments can face margin pressures. In Q1 2025, Energy Products revenue declined 4% and Chemical Products revenue fell 8%, largely due to falling refining margins and an oversupply in the global chemical market. Therefore, while high crude prices boost one side of the business, investors must monitor product solutions segment margins and overall production guidance during the Q1 2026 earnings call, expected in late April, to gauge the full impact. Beyond the immediate tailwinds from geopolitical tensions, Exxon Mobil's long-term investment thesis is underpinned by its strategic focus on "advantaged barrels" and robust production growth from key assets. The company's operations in Guyana, particularly the Stabroek block, are a cornerstone of this strategy. Projects like Uaru, expected to start up by year-end 2026 with a capacity of 250,000 b/d, and Whiptail, forecast to add another 250,000 b/d next year, are set to boost Guyana's daily oil production well beyond 1 million b/d. Exxon Mobil is also actively developing Guyana's significant recoverable gas resources, especially in the southeast part of the Stabroek block. The Hammerhead project, for instance, is designed to transport gas by pipeline to shore, complementing oil production. The company has already completed its first gas-to-energy pipeline, awaiting an onshore power plant to lower electricity costs in Guyana. This integrated approach to resource development highlights Exxon's commitment to maximizing value from its world-class geology and competitive development costs. The Permian Basin in the U.S. shale patch remains another critical growth engine. CEO Darren Woods has stated there is "no near-term peak Permian" for Exxon, citing over 40 technologies currently in testing to enhance recovery and efficiency. This focus on low-cost, high-margin production in both Guyana and the Permian has made XOM a "HALO" stock (Heavy-Asset, Low Obsolescence) for investors seeking stability and long-term value. Furthermore, Exxon Mobil's commitment to shareholder returns is a significant draw. The company has a strong track record of distributing capital through dividends and share repurchases, having distributed $9.4 billion in Q3 2025 and $9.5 billion in Q4 2025. As a dividend Aristocrat, boasting 26 consecutive annual dividend increases, XOM offers a compelling proposition for income-focused investors, signaling management's confidence in its ability to generate sustained free cash flow and maintain financial discipline. While Exxon Mobil benefits from current market dynamics, several significant risks could derail its long-term investment thesis. The most immediate concern remains commodity price volatility. Despite recent spikes, energy prices are inherently sensitive to geopolitical events, OPEC+ decisions, and global demand fluctuations. A sharp decline in prices, whether due to de-escalation in the Middle East, falling global demand, or oversupply, could significantly reduce ExxonMobil’s income, particularly in its highly profitable Upstream segment. Beyond oil prices, the company faces regulatory and political risks. Stricter environmental legislation globally, including potential bans on exploration in sensitive regions, new emissions standards, and tighter regulation of refining, could increase operating costs or limit production capacity. The accelerating global energy transition to lower-carbon sources poses a fundamental threat to long-term demand for fossil fuels, potentially diminishing Exxon Mobil's core product revenue streams and creating significant market risks. Exxon Mobil's diversified earnings are also susceptible to global chemical market oversupply and weak refining margins. As seen in Q1 2025, the chemical segment experienced substantial earnings reductions due to "bottom-of-cycle" margins. This cyclicality can act as a significant drag, even when other segments perform well. The capital-intensive nature of its upstream and downstream mix constrains revenue growth assumptions, keeping them modest at around 2.3%. Finally, valuation concerns persist among some analysts. With a TTM P/E ratio of 23.15 and a current price of $154.19, some models suggest the stock is trading at a premium. Analyst consensus price targets range around $140-$142, implying a modest downside from current levels. For instance, one model projects a $140.92 fair value, representing a 6% downside. While the company's beta of 0.35 reflects lower volatility than the broader market, a retreat in oil prices after tensions ease could expose valuation risks, making the stock less attractive at current levels. Navigating the current volatile energy market with Exxon Mobil requires a nuanced approach, balancing short-term tactical plays with long-term strategic considerations. For investors looking to capitalize on immediate geopolitical shocks, XOM's strong correlation with oil prices, coupled with its robust production and cash flow, makes it a compelling option. The stock's beta of 0.35 indicates lower volatility compared to the broader market, offering a degree of stability even in turbulent times. However, a purely short-term strategy is fraught with risk. The unpredictable nature of geopolitical events means any sudden de-escalation could lead to a sharp correction in oil prices and, consequently, in XOM's stock. Investors should consider XOM as a "HALO" stock, benefiting from heavy assets and low obsolescence, but remain vigilant. Monitoring key events like OPEC+ ministerial meetings for changes in production quotas, and geopolitical developments in critical regions like Guyana, is paramount. For long-term investors, Exxon Mobil's status as a dividend Aristocrat, with a current dividend yield of 2.6% and 26 consecutive annual increases, offers a compelling income component. This consistent return to shareholders, alongside disciplined capital allocation and share repurchase programs, provides a defensive moat against market fluctuations. The company's strategic investments in low-cost, high-return assets like the Permian and Guyana further solidify its long-term growth potential, irrespective of short-term price swings. To mitigate risks, diversification remains key. While XOM offers exposure to the energy sector, considering alternatives like ConocoPhillips (COP) for a more pure-play upstream focus, or Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ) for its strong inventory and capital discipline, could balance a portfolio. Ultimately, investors should maintain a conservative position sizing, perhaps 1% to 3% of their portfolio, given the stock's near-term volatility and the cyclical headwinds in its downstream and chemical segments. Exxon Mobil stands at a pivotal juncture, poised to benefit from current geopolitical tailwinds while navigating inherent industry volatility. Its strategic asset base and commitment to shareholder returns offer a compelling long-term narrative, but investors must remain acutely aware of the risks. title: Why Are BATL, TPET, XOM, CVX, USO, UCO Stocks Rising Overnight? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of multiple oil companies and oil exchange-traded funds climbed overnight late Sunday after Brent crude prices rose above $90 a barrel amid escalating tensions between the U.S. and Iran. Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, noted on X late Sunday, “Responding to this weekend's US-Iran escalation, Brent crude is currently above $90 a barrel in Asian trading.” WTI crude futures expiring in August also rose more than 2% to $84.33 per barrel. As a result, oil companies Battalion Oil Corp. (BATL) and Trio Petroleum Corp. (TPET) rose more than 7% and by over 8% in the overnight session. Oil majors Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) and Chevron Corp. (CVX) also rose about 1% each. Meanwhile, the United States Oil Fund (USO), which tracks the daily price movements of West Texas Intermediate (WTI), climbed more than 2% at the time of writing, while ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil (UCO) rallied more than 3%. The Light, Sweet Crude Oil Futures (CL_F) were also 2% higher. Oil prices soared back up as tensions between the U.S. and Iran escalated over the weekend after the American military launched a ninth consecutive night of attacks on the Middle Eastern country. “CENTCOM began conducting a new wave of strikes against Iran at 7 p.m. ET today for the ninth consecutive night. The strikes will continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz,” the U.S. Central Command said in a post on X. Over the weekend, CENTCOM confirmed that a third U.S. service member had died following recent fighting in the Middle East. The military had initially reported two fatalities and one service member missing after an Iranian attack in Jordan on July 17 before later confirming the third death. Meanwhile, Iran Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi condemned the U.S. strike on the under-construction Darquoin power plant, calling it a dangerous attack on Iran's civilian infrastructure. In a post on X, he said the strike made Washington fully responsible for the resulting instability and warned that Iran would take appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and interests. "The longer the Strait remains closed and the war escalates the greater ​the risk that oil prices will have to rise to around $150/barrel to bring demand down to match the hit to supply," Shane Oliver, Head of Investment Strategy and Chief Economist, at AMP reportedly told Reuters, adding that "This is not our base case but it's a high risk again." Meanwhile, Garfield Reynolds, MLIV Asia team leader at Bloomberg, reportedly said the widening spread between Brent crude and WTI reflects growing concerns that an escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict could disrupt global energy supplies, though the gap remains narrow enough that equity markets have largely shrugged off the risk compared with the early stages of the war. Analyst Patrick De Haan said on X that rising oil prices would likely send gas prices higher in the U.S. in the coming week. “Brent crude oil up ~3% reaching $90/bbl, while WTI crude up ~2% to nearly $85/bbl. RBOB up 5c/gal, national average gas price will hit $4/gal either tomorrow or Tuesday, likely to see increases ahead for most states!” he said. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BATL stock slipped from ‘extremely bullish’ to ‘bullish’ over 24 hours while it was in the ‘neutral’ territory for TPET. XOM and CVX stocks were trending in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing. Sentiment for USO and UCO stocks, meanwhile, was in the ‘extremely bullish’ and ‘bearish’ territories, respectively. One bullish user on Stocktwits said, “$USO $BATL I'm not selling, no matter what." BATL stock is up more than 46% this year, while TPET has declined nearly 60% in the same time. XOM and CVX have gained more than 20% each in 2026. AMD shares rose 1.3% in the overnight session late Sunday. A YAML code file by Anush Elangovan, a vice president of AI software at AMD, reportedly listed Anthropic as a “customer,” chip news site SemiAnalysis reported on Sunday. SemiAnalysis said Anthropic was assigned the maximum 30 “priority boost points,” placing it alongside existing hyperscale customers such as Meta – fueling speculation that AMD could formally announce a partnership with the AI startup at its flagship Advancing AI conference next week. “Note that Anthropic is still in the evaluation phase, and if AMD doesn’t announce Anthropic at its upcoming Advancing AI conference, that means @AnushElangovan’s FDE team has yet to address all of Anthropic’s concerns regarding software quality, and further improvement will be needed,” SemiAnalysis wrote. Meanwhile, Anthropic has reportedly been hiring engineers with ROCm experience (AMD’s AI software stack), suggesting it is preparing to further diversify its computing infrastructure, Jefferies analyst Blayne Curtis said in a recent note. Anthropic is not a publicly confirmed AMD customer. The AI startup has publicly said it trains and serves Claude using a mix of Nvidia GPUs, Amazon’s Trainium chips, and Google’s TPUs, with Amazon remaining its primary cloud and training partner. The AMD Advancing AI 2026 conference will run over Wednesday and Thursday at the Moscone Center in San Francisco. The company is expected to focus its announcements around AI infrastructure, new silicon-to-software pipelines, and enterprise-tier development. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for AMD remained ‘bullish,’ unchanged from the previous day, with traders noting speculation that Anthropic is becoming an AMD customer. “The recent market bloodbath just flushed $AMD from its 584 peak to the 490s. title: ExxonMobil (XOM), Chevron (CVX), ConocoPhillips (COP) Climb as Iran Tensions Drive Oil Rally - parameter.io
content: Oil prices advanced Wednesday following additional U.S. military operations against Iran, sparking heightened anxiety over potential interruptions to crude oil transport through the critical Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude momentarily peaked at $95 per barrel before settling at $94.40, representing a 3.7% increase. West Texas Intermediate contracts jumped nearly 4% to settle at $87.27. WTI has now registered gains exceeding 10% this week and stands more than 51% higher year-to-date. During remarks delivered in Manila, Secretary of State Marco Rubio characterized Iran as lacking genuine commitment to diplomatic engagement, though he emphasized the United States maintains willingness to pursue peaceful resolution. The Strait of Hormuz represents a critical chokepoint for global petroleum transport. Any significant interference at this location can rapidly constrain worldwide supply. “Markets are reestablishing a portion of the geopolitical risk premium,” explained Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com. She emphasized that market concerns extend beyond simple access questions to encompass shipping capacity, insurance expense escalation, and tanker fleet availability constraints. ExxonMobil and Chevron each climbed approximately 1.1% during premarket sessions. ConocoPhillips advanced 1.2%. ExxonMobil, commanding a market capitalization near $628 billion, operates an integrated structure encompassing upstream extraction, downstream refining operations, and petrochemical manufacturing. Wall Street analysts project approximately 10.7% appreciation potential from present levels, complemented by a 2.8% dividend yield. Chevron provides shareholders a 3.8% dividend return alongside analyst projections indicating roughly 13% upside potential. This balanced profile combining income generation and capital appreciation makes it attractive during periods of rising petroleum prices. ConocoPhillips maintains a more modest valuation relative to integrated competitors, trading at approximately 19.9 times earnings. Analysts identify the greatest appreciation opportunity among the trio at roughly 20.9%. Operating as a pure-play exploration and production entity, its financial performance correlates directly with crude price movements. All three corporations confront an identical primary challenge: demand erosion. Should WTI approach or exceed $100 per barrel, elevated prices could dampen economic activity and potentially trigger monetary policy responses from central banking authorities. WTI’s 52-week peak stands at $117.63. Market analysts indicate this threshold represents a potential inflection point where sentiment could transition from constructive to cautious. Refining sector equities Valero and Marathon Petroleum have both rocketed more than 92% year-to-date. Nevertheless, analysts currently identify limited additional upside, suggesting refining-linked opportunities may be fully valued at current levels. For the present, market attention centers on Middle Eastern developments. The ongoing confrontation between Washington and Tehran continues shaping energy market dynamics, with no diplomatic breakthrough apparent as of Wednesday morning trading. Safety performance will be one of the clearest measures of whether leaner operations are working effectively.
